karl-der-grosse#text: Charlemagne took over the Frankish kingdom in 768 and waged war almost every year: he defeated the Lombards, subdued the Saxons over thirty years and forced them to accept Christianity, and established a frontier march against the Muslims in Spain. In Aachen he founded a palace with a chapel that survives to this day, brought scholars such as Alcuin to his court, and promoted monasteries, schools, and scriptoria. Although he himself learned to write only with difficulty, we owe the transmission of many ancient texts to his educational reform. After his imperial coronation in 800 he was regarded in the Middle Ages as the model for all rulers.
wilhelm-der-eroberer#role: Duke of Normandy and King of England
wilhelm-der-eroberer#summary: The Norman duke who conquered England in 1066 and transformed the country profoundly.
wilhelm-der-eroberer#text: William was the illegitimate son of Duke Robert of Normandy and had to defend his rule against rivals from childhood on. With the victory at Hastings in 1066 he became King of England and in the following years put down revolts with great severity. He distributed the land to Norman followers, had castles such as the Tower of London built, and recorded the property and dues of the entire kingdom in the Domesday Book. His descendant sits on the English throne to this day.
dschingis-khan#summary: The steppe ruler who united the Mongols and founded the largest contiguous empire in history.
dschingis-khan#text: After the murder of his father, Temüjin grew up in poverty and captivity and rose through alliances and victories to become leader of all the Mongol tribes. As Genghis Khan he created a disciplined army, a communication system of mounted relays, and a law that punished theft and treason severely but granted freedom of religion. His campaigns cost millions of people their lives and destroyed flourishing cities in Central Asia and Persia. At his death in 1227 the empire stretched from the Pacific to the Caspian Sea; his grave has never been found.
mansa-musa#summary: The ruler of West Africa who, because of his gold-laden pilgrimage, is regarded as one of the richest people in history.
mansa-musa#text: Mansa Musa ruled from about 1312 to 1337 over the Mali Empire, which reached from the Atlantic to the bend of the Niger and controlled the gold and salt trade across the Sahara. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 made Mali's wealth known in the Islamic world and soon in Europe as well. He promoted education and Islam, had the Djinguereber Mosque built in Timbuktu, and made the city a center of scholarship with important collections of manuscripts. His empire did not break apart until the 15th century.
jeanne-darc#summary: The peasant girl from Lorraine who led the French army to victory at Orléans in the Hundred Years' War.
jeanne-darc#text: Joan grew up in Domrémy and was convinced that she had received from God the mission to free France from the English. At the age of seventeen she obtained an audience with the Dauphin Charles, received armor and troops, and in May 1429 relieved the besieged city of Orléans. After the coronation of Charles VII in Reims she fell into Burgundian captivity and was handed over to the English. A church court condemned her as a heretic; on May 30, 1431, she was burned in Rouen. In 1456 the verdict was annulled, and in 1920 she was canonized.
hildegard-von-bingen#summary: The Benedictine nun from the Rhine who worked as a visionary, naturalist, composer, and adviser to emperors and popes.
hildegard-von-bingen#text: As a child Hildegard was given into the hermitage of Disibodenberg and later led the community of women for which she founded a monastery of its own on the Rupertsberg near Bingen around 1150. In her principal work Scivias she described her visions, in works of natural history the healing effects of plants and stones, and she composed numerous sacred songs. She exchanged letters with Bernard of Clairvaux and Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and undertook several journeys as a preacher. In 2012 Pope Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church.
johannes-gutenberg#role: Inventor of printing with movable type
johannes-gutenberg#summary: The goldsmith from Mainz whose printing process revolutionized the spread of knowledge.
johannes-gutenberg#text: In Strasbourg and Mainz, Gutenberg developed a process in which letters were cast individually, assembled into pages, and printed with a press. His major work, the forty-two-line Bible, was produced around 1454. Because of debts he lost his workshop to his financier Johannes Fust and died without great wealth, yet his invention spread rapidly across all of Europe.
leonardo-da-vinci#summary: The universal genius of the Renaissance, who joined art and science.
leonardo-da-vinci#text: Leonardo was born in Tuscany and worked in Florence, Milan, Rome, and finally at the French royal court. His paintings the Mona Lisa and the Last Supper are among the best-known works of art in the world. On thousands of notebook pages he investigated anatomy, water, flight, and mechanics and designed machines far ahead of their time.
christoph-kolumbus#summary: The Genoese navigator who reached America in 1492 while searching for India.
christoph-kolumbus#text: After years of effort, Columbus persuaded the Spanish monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand to finance a voyage westward. On four voyages he explored the Caribbean and the coasts of Central and South America. As governor of the new colonies he acted harshly against the native population and in 1500 was brought back to Spain in chains for misrule.
nikolaus-kopernikus#summary: The founder of the heliocentric worldview, which moved the earth out of the center of the universe.
nikolaus-kopernikus#text: Copernicus was born in Thorn, studied in Kraków and Italy, and served as a canon in Frauenburg in Warmia. Alongside his church and administrative duties he observed the sky and calculated a model in which the earth turns daily on its own axis and annually around the sun. He published his principal work only in 1543, the year of his death.
martin-luther#summary: The Augustinian monk whose criticism of the sale of indulgences set off the Reformation.
martin-luther#text: Luther taught as a professor of theology in Wittenberg and came to the conviction that a person is made righteous before God by faith and grace alone, not by good works or indulgences. After the break with Rome he translated the Bible into German and thereby shaped the German written language. He wrote catechisms and hymns, but condemned the rebellious peasants and in late writings expressed himself with hatred against Jews.
elisabeth-i#summary: The Tudor queen under whom England rose to become a Protestant naval and trading power.
elisabeth-i#text: Elizabeth, daughter of Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, came to the throne in 1558 and established the Anglican Church as a middle way between Catholicism and Calvinism. In 1588 the Spanish Armada failed in its attempt to conquer England. Her 45-year reign is regarded as a golden age of poetry and theater with William Shakespeare and as the beginning of English overseas expansion. Since she remained unmarried, the Tudor dynasty ended with her.
george-washington#role: Commander in chief and first President of the United States
george-washington#summary: The leader in the War of Independence who shaped the United States as its first president.
george-washington#text: The plantation owner from Virginia led the Continental Army from 1775 and held it together despite defeats, hunger, and desertions, until the victory at Yorktown in 1781 decided the war. In 1787 he presided over the Constitutional Convention and in 1789 was unanimously elected the first president. After two terms he gave up power voluntarily and thereby set a standard for republican government. Until his death he owned slaves, whom he freed in his will.
olympe-de-gouges#role: Writer and advocate of women's rights
olympe-de-gouges#summary: The author of the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, who went to the guillotine for her convictions.
olympe-de-gouges#text: Marie Gouze from Montauban came to Paris as a young widow, where she wrote plays and political texts and campaigned against slavery. In 1791 her Declaration demanded the same rights for women as for men, and she wrote that if a woman has the right to mount the scaffold, she must also have the right to mount the speaker's platform. Because she attacked the Jacobins and called for a popular vote on the form of the state, she was executed in November 1793.
maximilien-de-robespierre#role: Jacobin leader and member of the Committee of Public Safety
maximilien-de-robespierre#summary: The Incorruptible, who sought to defend the revolution with terror and ended under the guillotine himself.
maximilien-de-robespierre#text: The lawyer from Arras argued in the National Assembly for universal suffrage and against the death penalty, but from 1793 became the driving force of the Reign of Terror. In the name of virtue he had opponents such as the Girondins and Danton executed and introduced a cult of the Supreme Being. On July 27, 1794, the Convention and his former allies overthrew him; one day later he was guillotined.
toussaint-louverture#summary: The former slave who led Saint-Domingue to the abolition of slavery and to the threshold of independence.
toussaint-louverture#text: Toussaint was born a slave on a plantation and was freed before the revolution. After the uprising of 1791 he rose to become the ablest general of the insurgents, defeated the Spanish and the British, and from 1801 governed the colony with a constitution of his own as governor for life. Napoleon sent an army against him; Toussaint was captured through betrayal and died in 1803 in a fortress in the French Jura. His successor Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti in 1804.
napoleon-bonaparte#summary: The Corsican who conquered and reordered Europe as a commander and emperor.
napoleon-bonaparte#text: Napoleon was born in Ajaccio, rose quickly to general in the revolutionary wars, and seized power in 1799 through a coup. As emperor he won victories such as Austerlitz in 1805 and Jena in 1806, spread the Code civil, and dissolved the Holy Roman Empire. The Russian campaign of 1812 and the defeats at Leipzig and Waterloo ended his rule; he died in 1821 in exile on St. Helena.
simon-bolivar#role: South American freedom fighter and statesman
simon-bolivar#summary: The Libertador, who freed large parts of South America from Spanish rule.
simon-bolivar#text: Bolívar came from a wealthy family in Caracas and was shaped in Europe by the ideas of the Enlightenment. After several setbacks he led campaigns from 1819 that liberated Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, which was named after him. His dream of a united South American republic failed because of civil wars and regional interests; embittered, he died in 1830 on his way into exile.
hannibal#summary: Rome's most dangerous opponent, who crossed the Alps with elephants.
hannibal#text: In the Second Punic War, Hannibal led his army from Spain across the Alps into Italy and in 216 BC won at Cannae one of the greatest victories in military history. Even so, he was unable to take Rome. After the defeat at Zama he went into exile and took his own life so as not to fall into Roman hands.
cicero#summary: Rome's most famous orator and a defender of the republic.
cicero#text: As consul in 63 BC, Cicero uncovered the conspiracy of Catiline. His speeches, letters, and philosophical writings shaped the Latin language and European education into the modern era. After Caesar's death he opposed Mark Antony and was murdered on his orders.
gaius-julius-caesar#summary: Conqueror of Gaul, victor in the civil war, and forerunner of the imperial age.
gaius-julius-caesar#text: Caesar rose to power through the triumvirate with Pompey and Crassus, conquered Gaul, and in 49 BC crossed the Rubicon with the words Alea iacta est. As dictator he reformed the calendar and the administration. His murder on the Ides of March in 44 BC did not end the republic but accelerated its downfall.
augustus#summary: Caesar's adopted son Octavian, who as Augustus founded the imperial age.
augustus#text: After Caesar's death, Octavian prevailed against Antony and Cleopatra and in 27 BC received the title Augustus, the exalted one. He reorganized the army, the provinces, and the finances, had Rome adorned with marble buildings, and secured four decades of peace. The month of August bears his name.
konstantin-der-grosse#summary: The first Christian emperor and founder of Constantinople.
konstantin-der-grosse#text: Constantine prevailed in 312 at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, reportedly under the sign of the cross. He ended the persecution of Christians, convened the Council of Nicaea, and in 330 made the old Byzantium, as Constantinople, the new capital of the empire.
lucy#summary: The most famous fossil of an upright-walking hominin, found in Ethiopia in 1974.
lucy#text: Lucy was discovered in 1974 by a team around Donald Johanson at Hadar in Ethiopia and named after the Beatles song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds. About 40 percent of her roughly 3.2-million-year-old skeleton is preserved. She was about 1.05 meters tall and had a small brain, but already walked upright on two legs. She thus shows that upright walking arose long before the growth of the brain.
oetzi#role: Glacier mummy from the Copper Age
oetzi#summary: The best-preserved human being of the Neolithic, found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991.
oetzi#text: Ötzi was about 45 years old, around 1.60 meters tall, and bore more than 60 tattoos. He died around 3300 BC from an arrow shot and was preserved by the glacier ice. His equipment, with a copper axe, bow, flint dagger, backpack frame, and birch-bark containers, is the most complete surviving set from this period. Today he lies in the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano.
neandertaler#summary: A cold-adapted human species that inhabited Europe and western Asia and disappeared about 40,000 years ago.
neandertaler#text: Neanderthals developed in Europe about 400,000 years ago and lived as far as Siberia and the Near East. They were powerfully built, had a large brain, hunted big game, used fire, cared for the sick, and buried their dead. They are named after the find of 1856 in the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. About 40,000 years ago they died out; a small part of their genetic heritage, however, lives on in present-day people outside Africa.
adolf-hitler#summary: Leader of the Nazi Party and chiefly responsible for the Second World War and the Holocaust.
adolf-hitler#text: Born in Austria, Hitler took over the leadership of the Nazi Party after the First World War and failed with an attempted coup in Munich in 1923. He set down his ideology of racism, antisemitism, and lust for conquest in Mein Kampf. After his appointment as chancellor in 1933 he established a totalitarian dictatorship, unleashed the war in 1939, and ordered the murder of Europe's Jews. Facing defeat, he took his own life in Berlin on April 30, 1945.
winston-churchill#summary: Led Great Britain from 1940 in the fight against Hitler and refused any compromise.
winston-churchill#text: Churchill had warned about Hitler as early as the 1930s and became prime minister in May 1940, in the gravest crisis. When France fell and German bombers attacked British cities, he embodied the country's will to hold out; his speeches promised nothing but blood, toil, tears, and sweat. Together with Roosevelt and Stalin he planned the conduct of the war and the postwar order. In 1953 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical works.
franklin-d-roosevelt#summary: Led the United States out of the Great Depression and through the war at the side of the Allies.
franklin-d-roosevelt#text: Roosevelt, confined to a wheelchair since a bout of polio, was elected in 1932 and fought the economic crisis with the New Deal. He supported Great Britain with arms deliveries even before entering the war and, after Pearl Harbor, made the United States the arsenal of democracy. At the conferences of Tehran and Yalta he laid the foundations of the postwar order and of the United Nations together with Churchill and Stalin. He died in April 1945, a few weeks before victory, as the only president elected four times.
josef-stalin#summary: Ruled the Soviet Union through terror and led it to victory over Germany.
josef-stalin#text: After Lenin's death, Stalin prevailed against all rivals and forced the country to industrialize with five-year plans and compulsory collectivization; millions died through hunger, deportations, and the purges of the 1930s. In 1939 he concluded a pact with Hitler and divided Poland. After the German attack in 1941 he organized the resistance and, through victory, became master of Eastern Europe, where he installed communist dictatorships.
anne-frank#summary: Her diary from the hiding place in Amsterdam became the world's best-known testimony of the Holocaust.
anne-frank#text: Born in Frankfurt, Anne Frank fled with her family from the National Socialists to Amsterdam in 1934. From July 1942 the family lived hidden in the annex of a company building, where Anne wrote her diary. In August 1944 those in hiding were betrayed and deported by way of Auschwitz to the Bergen-Belsen camp, where Anne died of typhus in the spring of 1945 at the age of 15. Her father Otto, the only one who survived, published the diary in 1947.
sophie-scholl#role: Resistance fighter of the White Rose
sophie-scholl#summary: Distributed leaflets against the Nazi regime together with her brother Hans and was executed for it.
sophie-scholl#text: The Munich student Sophie Scholl joined the resistance group White Rose around her brother Hans in 1942, which denounced the crimes of the regime in leaflets and called for resistance. On February 18, 1943, the siblings were discovered and arrested while laying out leaflets in the university. Four days later the People's Court under Roland Freisler sentenced them to death; they were beheaded the same day. The White Rose is regarded today as a symbol of moral courage.
galileo-galilei#summary: The founder of experimental natural science, who explored the sky with the telescope and came into conflict with the church for it.
galileo-galilei#text: Galileo taught in Pisa and Padua and investigated the laws of free fall and of the pendulum through experiments on the inclined plane. In 1609 he built a telescope of his own and discovered the mountains of the moon, four moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, and sunspots, which he published in 1610 in the Starry Messenger. His observations supported the worldview of Copernicus, which the church banned in 1616; the trial of 1633 ended with recantation and house arrest. He wrote his works in Italian rather than Latin in order to reach a broad public, and is regarded as the father of modern physics.
john-locke#summary: The English thinker whose doctrine of natural rights and government by consent founded liberalism.
john-locke#text: Locke studied medicine at Oxford and became physician, secretary, and adviser to the Earl of Shaftesbury, an opponent of the king; because of political persecution he lived in exile in the Netherlands from 1683 to 1689. After the Glorious Revolution he published the Two Treatises of Government, the Letter Concerning Toleration, and the Essay Concerning Human Understanding. He taught that the mind is a blank slate at birth and that all knowledge comes from experience. His demand for the protection of life, liberty, and property became the foundation of American and European constitutional states.
maria-theresia#role: Archduchess of Austria, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia
maria-theresia#summary: The only woman at the head of the Habsburg monarchy, who defended her inheritance in war and reformed the state fundamentally.
maria-theresia#text: Maria Theresa took over a threatened inheritance in 1740 at the age of 23 and lost Silesia to Prussia, but held on to her remaining lands. With her ministers Haugwitz and Kaunitz she created a central administration, a standing army, a new tax system that also burdened the nobility, and, in 1774, compulsory schooling for all. She was devout, rejected religious tolerance, and abolished torture only in 1776. With her husband Francis Stephen she had 16 children, among them Emperor Joseph II and the later French queen Marie Antoinette.
jean-jacques-rousseau#summary: The Geneva thinker who established the idea of popular sovereignty and criticized civilization as a source of inequality.
jean-jacques-rousseau#text: Rousseau grew up in Geneva as the son of a watchmaker, made his way as a private tutor, music copyist, and secretary, and became famous in 1750 with a prize essay claiming that the sciences and arts had corrupted morals. In 1762 there appeared the Social Contract, according to which only the general will of the people may give laws, and the educational novel Émile, which sought to let the child develop according to its nature. Both books were banned in Paris and Geneva, and Rousseau lived on the run from then on. His Confessions founded the modern autobiography; the Jacobins revered him as a prophet of the revolution.
emilie-du-chatelet#summary: The French scholar who translated and explained Newton's Principia and was one of the first women to help shape the physics of her time.
emilie-du-chatelet#text: As the daughter of a court official, Gabrielle Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil received an unusually good education and later had herself taught by the mathematicians Maupertuis and Clairaut. At her château at Cirey she set up a laboratory and a library with Voltaire, her companion; her Institutions de physique of 1740 combined Newton's mechanics with the philosophy of Leibniz. She recognized that the energy of motion of a body increases with the square of its velocity. She completed her annotated translation of the Principia shortly before her death in childbirth; it remains the authoritative French version to this day.
katharina-die-grosse#summary: The German princess who became tsarina through a coup, enlarged Russia, and presented herself as an enlightened ruler.
katharina-die-grosse#text: Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst was married to the Russian heir to the throne in 1745, adopted the Orthodox faith and the name Catherine, and in 1762 overthrew her incompetent husband Peter III with the help of the guard. She corresponded with Voltaire, bought Diderot's library, and in 1767 presented a legislative commission with an instruction based on the ideas of Montesquieu and Beccaria, which nonetheless had no consequences. After the uprising of peasants and Cossacks under Pugachev in 1773 she strengthened the nobility and extended serfdom. Through wars against the Ottomans and the partitions of Poland, Russia gained the Crimea, the Black Sea coast, and extensive territories in the west.
tokugawa-ieyasu#summary: The commander who united Japan after the victory at Sekigahara and established an order of peace that lasted 250 years.
tokugawa-ieyasu#text: Ieyasu first served Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi and during this time built a strong power base in eastern Japan around Edo Castle, in present-day Tokyo. After Hideyoshi's death he defeated the rival lords at Sekigahara in the year 1600 and in 1603 had himself appointed shogun by the emperor. He bound the lords to obedience, ordered the estates of samurai, peasants, artisans, and merchants, and began to suppress Christianity. His descendants ruled Japan until 1868; the Edo period brought peace, the growth of cities, and a flourishing culture with kabuki theater and woodblock printing.
sappho#summary: The most important lyric poet of antiquity, whose love poems from the island of Lesbos led even the Greeks to celebrate her as the tenth Muse.
sappho#text: Sappho lived around 600 BC in Mytilene on Lesbos and came from a noble family that had to go into exile in Sicily for a time. She gathered around her young women whom she taught in music and poetry, and wrote songs for the lyre about love, longing, jealousy, weddings, and the goddess Aphrodite. Of her nine books only a single complete poem and many fragments survive, some discovered only in the 20th century on papyrus from Egypt. Plato called her the tenth Muse; the Sapphic stanza named after her was taken up by Horace and many later poets.
herodot#summary: The father of history, who described the Persian Wars and the peoples of his time.
herodot#text: Herodotus came from Halicarnassus in Asia Minor, traveled through Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Black Sea region, and Greece, and lived for periods in Athens and in the colony of Thurii in southern Italy. In the nine books of his Histories he set out to explain why Greeks and Persians went to war, and in doing so described the lands, customs, religions, and marvels of the world known to him, from the pyramids to the Scythians. He distinguished between what he had seen, what he had heard, and what he merely supposed, even though he took over many accounts without checking them. Cicero called him the father of history; his work is at the same time the first work of ethnography.
aspasia#summary: The educated woman from Miletus who moved in the circles of Socrates and Pericles in Athens and is said to have taught orators.
aspasia#text: Aspasia came to Athens from Miletus in Asia Minor and lived as a metic, a foreigner without citizenship, together with Pericles, who had separated from his wife; their son later received citizenship as an exception. Her house became a meeting place for philosophers and artists, and in one dialogue Plato has Socrates claim that she taught him the art of speaking and composed speeches for Pericles. The comic poets mocked her as a courtesan and blamed her for the Peloponnesian War, and she is said to have been charged with impiety. Aspasia is one of the few examples of a woman who exercised public influence in the Athens of the 5th century BC.
hippokrates#summary: The most famous physician of antiquity and founder of a medicine based on observation and natural causes.
hippokrates#text: Hippocrates was born around 460 BC on the island of Kos into a family of physicians who traced their art back to the healing god Asclepius. He traveled through Greece as an itinerant physician, taught on Kos, and was already so famous in his lifetime that Plato mentions him. The writings handed down under his name come from various physicians of his school, yet they share his principles: careful observation, caution with interventions, trust in the healing power of nature, and the rejection of magic. The Hippocratic oath and the principle above all of doing no harm make him a model for physicians to this day.
demosthenes#summary: The greatest orator of Athens, who fought in vain against Philip of Macedon for the freedom of the Greek cities.
